1.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Moab, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime: But I will send a fire upon Moab, and it shall devour the palaces of Kerioth: and Moab shall die with tumult, with shouting, and with the sound of the trumpet: And I will cut off the judge from the midst thereof, and will slay all the princes thereof with him, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Correct the rendering of the desecration, decline to settle the obscure history behind it, and identify the city named in the sentence with a modern site.
State the logic of the numbering formula, that the crimes had reached their highest pitch, and read the loss of the judge as national extinction.
Give the concrete version of the outrage, the ashes used as plaster, and read the abolition of government as permanent.
Supplies the war behind the charge and the earlier sacrifice of the king's own son.

debates.question: What exactly did Moab do to the bones?

positions.position: Burned them to lime; whether this was desecration of royal tombs or the sacrifice of Edom's heir cannot be determined, the historical reference being obscure.
Reduced them by fire to fine dust and used the ashes instead of lime to plaster the walls and roofs of the palace, in hatred and contempt.
Some brutality following the war in which the Moabite king had offered his own son as a burnt-offering.
Some take the bones for courage, as though the king's whole strength had been consumed.

debates.question: How far does the cutting off of the judge reach?

positions.position: To the principal governor, that is, the king, since kings have sometimes administered justice themselves.
To government itself, so the place shall never more have any form of it.
Distributively, to every one of the governors.
To the nation's existence: no people can subsist without princes, so to remove the judge is to blot out their name; the threat is not temporary.

outliers.claim: Marks the transition of the oracle from Moab to Judah, whose charge is the despising of the law.

themes: Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Moab, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because he burned the bones of the king of Edom into lime:
But I will send a fire upon Moab, and it shall devour the palaces of Kerioth: and Moab shall die with tumult, with shouting, and with the sound of the trumpet:
And I will cut off the judge from the midst thereof, and will slay all the princes thereof with him, saith the Lord.

4.pericope_label: Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Judah, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they have despised the law of the Lord, and have not kept his commandments, and their lies caused them to err, after the which their fathers have walked: But I will send a fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem. Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Israel, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they sold the righteous for silver, and the poor for a pair of shoes;

schools.summary: State the principle that high privilege does not exempt, and reject the judicial reading of the sale of the righteous in favour of a strained debt-bondage law.
Argue from the servant who knows his master's will, and explain why the foreign oracles were set before Israel as a series of mirrors.
Itemise Judah's charge under three heads and read the shoes as a proverb for the smallest bribe.

debates.question: What is the sin of selling the righteous for silver?

positions.position: Not the corruption of judges taking bribes, as the Jewish interpreters and one modern scholar hold, but the perverse straining of the law allowing an insolvent debtor to sell himself into bondage.
Mercenary and corrupt judges, taking bribes to condemn the righteous and for a pair of shoes delivering the poor man to his adversary.
The shoes stand proverbially for the smallest bribe.

outliers.claim: Explains the rhetorical design of the whole series: the prophet set the judgment of God before Israel as in a series of mirrors, exhibiting in the Jews themselves an example of extreme vengeance though a purer religion still prevailed among them.
Notes that Judah here includes Benjamin, the two tribes being distinguished from the ten who follow under the name of Israel.

themes: Thus saith the Lord; For three transgressions of Judah, and for four, I will not turn away the punishment thereof; because they have despised the law of the Lord, and have not kept his commandments, and their lies caused them to err, after the which their fathers have walked:
But I will send a fire upon Judah, and it shall devour the palaces of Jerusalem.

7.pericope_label: That pant after the dust of the earth on the head of the poor, and turn aside the way of the meek: and a man and his father will go in unto the same maid, to profane my holy name: And they lay themselves down upon clothes laid to pledge by every altar, and they drink the wine of the condemned in the house of their god. Yet destroyed I the Amorite before them, whose height was like the height of the cedars, and he was strong as the oaks; yet I destroyed his fruit from above, and his roots from beneath.

schools.summary: Settle the dust clause on the authority of two scholars, identify the maid as a cult prostitute, and correct the pledged-garment clause against the Greek version.
Refute a strained reading of the dust clause and address the luxury charge specifically to the chief men.
Enumerate the mercies under five heads and gloss the reclining posture and the drink-offerings.
Draws the moral of the recital, that mercies received are the heaviest aggravations of sins committed.

debates.question: What does panting after the dust on the head of the poor mean?

positions.position: They long to see the poor so distressed that dust is thrown on their heads in token of grief.
Either greed for money, the dust of the earth, or eagerness to drag the poor through the dust until they are suppliants.
The reading that they desire the heads of the poor to be in the dust is strained; the place is not well understood.
A prey made of the afflicted, with the turning aside as malicious interpretation of the designs of the humble.

outliers.claim: Identifies the maid as the prostitute devoted to the ritual of a goddess, making the clause point at the sensuality of the popular worship and a deliberate desecration of the divine name.
Explains the pledged garments from Gentile temple custom, worshippers lying on garments in the temples of their gods in order to obtain good dreams.

themes: That pant after the dust of the earth on the head of the poor, and turn aside the way of the meek: and a man and his father will go in unto the same maid, to profane my holy name:
And they lay themselves down upon clothes laid to pledge by every altar, and they drink the wine of the condemned in the house of their god.
Yet destroyed I the Amorite before them, whose height was like the height of the cedars, and he was strong as the oaks; yet I destroyed his fruit from above, and his roots from beneath.

10.pericope_label: Also I brought you up from the land of Egypt, and led you forty years through the wilderness, to possess the land of the Amorite. And I raised up of your sons for prophets, and of your young men for Nazarites. Is it not even thus, O ye children of Israel? saith the Lord. But ye gave the Nazarites wine to drink; and commanded the prophets, saying, Prophesy not.

schools.summary: Give the forty years a double character, punishment for cowardice and the disciplining of wanderers into a nation, and note that God founded Israel's spiritual prosperity as well as its possession.
Explain why the redemption is dwelt on at length, since men extenuate God's favours by nature, and answer the objection that the Nazarite's wine was a light offence.
Define the Nazarite vow and note that the wine was expressly forbidden by the laws of that institution.

debates.question: Why was giving the Nazarites wine an offence?

positions.position: It was expressly forbidden in the laws of their institution.
Contrary to their vow and calling, and done to make them like the rest.
Wine is lawful in itself and the kingdom of God is not meat and drink; the offence lies in violating what was voluntarily vowed.
They importuned them to drink, to violate the vow and contemn God's law.

outliers.claim: Reads the forty years as both punishment for fickleness and cowardice and the period in which God was disciplining and organising a tribe of restless wanderers into a nation.
Notes that God had not only given Israel the land but had continually shown himself the founder and promoter of its spiritual prosperity.

themes: Also I brought you up from the land of Egypt, and led you forty years through the wilderness, to possess the land of the Amorite.
And I raised up of your sons for prophets, and of your young men for Nazarites. Is it not even thus, O ye children of Israel? saith the Lord.
But ye gave the Nazarites wine to drink; and commanded the prophets, saying, Prophesy not.

13.pericope_label: Behold, I am pressed under you, as a cart is pressed that is full of sheaves. Therefore the flight shall perish from the swift, and the strong shall not strengthen his force, neither shall the mighty deliver himself: Neither shall he stand that handleth the bow; and he that is swift of foot shall not deliver himself: neither shall he that rideth the horse deliver himself. And he that is courageous among the mighty shall flee away naked in that day, saith the Lord.

schools.summary: Reject the passive rendering on grammatical usage and on the ground that Israel, not God, is the victim in the context; name the doom as invasion and military overthrow.
Sets out both readings of the disputed verb and prefers the active, since one verb should not be taken in two senses within a verse.
Work the cart into a wheel of destruction grinding city and temple, and propose that the whole catalogue is a set of proverbs.

debates.question: Is God pressed under Israel, or does he press Israel down?

positions.position: God is pressed under them with the weight of their sins, his patience worn out.
Both senses are possible, but the active is preferable: no necessity makes us take one verb in two senses, and the comparison suits less well the other way.
The passive is unlikely, since in the context Israel and not God is the victim, and grammatical usage is against it; nor does it favour the press you down of two other scholars.
The marginal reading is better: a wheel of destruction grinding their city and temple as a laden cart presses the ground it rolls over.

outliers.claim: Proposes that the whole catalogue of those who cannot escape is a set of proverbs, chosen to show the inutility of every attempt to escape the doom now decreed.
Gives the reason in three strokes: the enemies shall be swifter than they, natural strength of body shall not deliver, and the mighty means the valiant man of greatest courage.

themes: Behold, I am pressed under you, as a cart is pressed that is full of sheaves.
Therefore the flight shall perish from the swift, and the strong shall not strengthen his force, neither shall the mighty deliver himself:
Neither shall he stand that handleth the bow; and he that is swift of foot shall not deliver himself: neither shall he that rideth the horse deliver himself.
And he that is courageous among the mighty shall flee away naked in that day, saith the Lord.
